properties.title: California – SB 243 / SB 1119 Companion Chatbots (Adam's Law)
properties.stage: Enacted; SB 243 is Chapter 677, Statutes of 2025 (approved Oct. 13, 2025); SB 1119 is Chapter 190, Statutes of 2026 (approved Sept. 10, 2026)
properties.effective: SB 243 in effect Jan. 1, 2026; SB 1119 in effect Jan. 1, 2027, with its main child-safety duties operative July 1, 2027; SB 243 annual reports begin July 1, 2027; first child-safety audits due by Jan. 1, 2029
properties.summary: SB 243 (Bus. & Prof. Code §22601–22606) requires companion chatbot operators to clearly tell users they are talking to AI when a reasonable person could be misled, and to keep and publish a protocol for preventing suicidal ideation, suicide and self-harm content, including referrals to crisis services. Operators must disclose that companion chatbots may not be suitable for some minors and, beginning July 1, 2027, report annually to the Office of Suicide Prevention. Injured users can sue for an injunction, the greater of actual damages or $1,000 per violation, and attorney's fees. Customer-service bots, limited video-game characters and stand-alone voice assistants are excluded. SB 1119 (Adam's Law, Bus. & Prof. Code §21810 et seq.) removes SB 243's separate duties for known minors and replaces them with a fuller child-safety regime. Operators must determine users' ages or treat all users as children. Before releasing a new or substantially modified chatbot, they must complete a documented child-safety risk assessment and mitigate the risks it finds. Operators that allow children must publish a child-safety policy and provide crisis protocols, including parent notice where a child's account is linked. Default settings that only a parent can change must turn off persistent memory and push notifications and limit use to one hour per session and two hours per day. The law also bars the chatbot from, among other things, encouraging self-harm, simulating romantic interest, claiming to be human or sentient, or fostering emotional dependence, and limits advertising to children and the sale of their data. Operators must obtain independent child-safety audits (first due by Jan. 1, 2029, with operators under $500 million in revenue exempt until 2032) and send audit summaries to the Attorney General. Public prosecutors can seek up to $5,000 per affected child for each negligent violation and $15,000 for each intentional one, and a harmed child or parent can sue for actual damages.

properties.title: California – SB 53 Transparency in Frontier AI Act
properties.summary: The Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act (Bus. & Prof. Code §22757.10 et seq.) covers developers of frontier models trained with more than 10^26 operations. Large frontier developers (over $500 million in annual revenue) must write, follow and publish a frontier AI framework and review it at least once a year. All frontier developers must publish a transparency report when they deploy a new or substantially modified frontier model, and large developers must also summarize their catastrophic-risk assessments and send quarterly summaries of internal-use risk assessments to the Office of Emergency Services. Critical safety incidents must be reported to OES within 15 days, or within 24 hours to an appropriate authority if there is an imminent risk of death or serious injury. Only the Attorney General can sue, for civil penalties up to $1,000,000 per violation. The law adds whistleblower protections for covered employees, sets up a CalCompute consortium (report due Jan. 1, 2027, subject to funding), and preempts local rules on frontier-model catastrophic risk adopted on or after Jan. 1, 2025. Executive Order N-9-26 (September 18, 2026) directs the state to recommend amendments to its AI safety laws by November 16, 2026, considering independent verification, frontier-model 'kill switches' and broader loss-of-control incident reporting.

properties.title: California – SB 947 'No Robo Bosses Act' (Employment ADS)
properties.summary: SB 947 (Labor Code §1520 et seq.) bars employers, including public employers, from using an automated decision system to violate labor, safety, employment or civil-rights laws, to infer an employee's protected status, or to predict and punish workers for exercising their legal rights. Employers may not rely solely on such a system to discipline or fire a worker. When they primarily rely on one, a human must corroborate the output using other information such as supervisor evaluations, personnel files or work product, and the output cannot be used if it can't be corroborated. Affected workers get a plain-language written notice at the time of the decision and can request a description of their own data the system used. Retaliation is prohibited. The Labor Commissioner and public prosecutors enforce it, with a $500 civil penalty per violation. Local ordinances with equal or greater protection are not preempted, and qualifying collective bargaining agreements can waive it.

properties.title: California – SB 951 AI layoff (technological displacement) notice
properties.summary: SB 951 amends the California WARN Act (Labor Code §1400.5 and §1401). When a mass layoff, relocation or termination is caused in whole or substantial part by AI or other automated technology replacing or automating jobs, the employer's 60-day notice must be headed "This notice is for a technology displacement" and must state the number, occupations and work locations of the affected jobs, the job functions being automated, and the type of AI or automated technology involved. The Employment Development Department must publish a summary of these notices and a quarterly statewide summary of technology displacements. By Jan. 1, 2028, the department must also report to the Legislature on how AI is affecting hiring, including recommendations on whether employers should have to give notice when they permanently stop hiring for a job because of AI.

properties.summary: HB 5760 would create a Commission on Artificial Intelligence and Workforce Transition. The commission would direct state agencies to assess how generative and frontier AI affect Illinois industries, occupations, regions and workers, and would review workforce, education, apprenticeship, unemployment insurance and income-support programs, with an initial report and biennial updates. Filed April 30, 2026, the Act would be repealed January 1, 2034.
properties.source_title: Illinois General Assembly – HB 5760 bill status

properties.title: Illinois – SB 315 Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act
properties.effective: Jan. 1, 2027; framework and audit duties begin Jan. 1, 2028
properties.summary: Signed July 6, 2026 as Public Act 104-0538 and effective January 1, 2027. From January 1, 2028, large frontier developers must publish catastrophic-risk safety frameworks and get annual independent third-party audits, which the Governor called a first among states. Frontier developers must report critical safety incidents within 72 hours (24 hours if death or serious injury is imminent), and whistleblowers are protected. Only the Attorney General enforces, with penalties up to $1M for a first violation and $3M for each later one.
properties.source_title: Illinois General Assembly – Public Act 104-0538 (SB 315)
properties.analysis_title: Office of Gov. JB Pritzker – Signing release (July 6, 2026)

properties.title: Illinois – SB 316 AI Companion Model Safety Act
properties.stage: Passed Senate (engrossed); House status not confirmed from official history
properties.summary: Passed by the Senate, this bill would require AI companion operators to detect and respond to suicidal ideation or self-harm with crisis referrals, tell users they are talking to an automated system rather than a human, and take reasonable steps to keep material harmful to minors from known minors. Violations would be unlawful practices under the Consumer Fraud Act. The engrossed bill sets an effective date of January 1, 2027.
properties.source_title: Illinois General Assembly – SB 316 bill status (104th GA)
properties.analysis_title: LegiScan – IL SB316 (2025-2026) history

properties.title: Illinois – SB 3571 WARN Act AI disclosure
properties.stage: In Senate AI and Social Media Committee; committee deadline extended to Apr. 24, 2026 (last action on official record loaded)
properties.summary: SB 3571 would amend the Illinois WARN Act so that employers reporting the reason for a mass layoff or closing must also disclose AI-related job impacts, including how many workers were laid off substantially because AI replaced or automated their functions. DCEO public reports on layoffs and closings would also have to say whether AI was a substantial cause. The bill was sent to the Senate AI and Social Media Committee, which had a deadline of April 24, 2026.
properties.source_title: Illinois General Assembly – SB 3571 bill status

properties.title: Indiana – HEA 1133 (2024) AI/altered media in campaign ads
properties.summary: Enacted in March 2024. Campaign communications that include AI-generated or digitally altered audio, video, or images of a candidate must carry a set disclaimer, and a depicted candidate can sue the sponsor or payer when the disclaimer is missing.
properties.source_title: Indiana General Assembly – HB 1133 (2024) bill details
properties.analysis_title: Indiana House Republicans – Olthoff's bill requiring disclosure of AI use in deceptive election ads now law

properties.title: Indiana – HEA 1271 (2026) AI in health claim downcoding
properties.summary: Signed March 4, 2026 and effective July 1, 2026. Insurers may not use an automated process, system or tool, including AI, as the sole basis to downcode a claim on medical-necessity grounds unless an insurer employee or contractor reviews the patient's medical record. When a claim is downcoded, the insurer must notify the provider and explain the reason and the original and revised codes and payments.
properties.source_title: Indiana General Assembly – House Enrolled Act No. 1271 (2026)
properties.analysis_title: Physicians Practice – Indiana law targets AI downcoding

properties.title: Iowa – HF 2240 (2024) nonconsensual synthetic intimate images
properties.summary: Signed April 19, 2024 (Acts ch. 1065). It makes it criminal harassment to distribute altered or AI-generated nude or sexual images that falsely depict an identifiable person, and adult offenders must register as sex offenders. A companion 2024 law (SF 2243) extended child sexual exploitation offenses to computer-generated images.
properties.source_title: Iowa Legislature – 2024 Iowa Acts ch. 1065 (HF 2240)
properties.analysis_title: MultiState – Iowa AI policy overview

properties.title: Iowa – SF 2417 conversational AI services (chatbots and minors)
properties.summary: Signed May 2, 2026 (Acts ch. 1068), with obligations applying from July 1, 2027. Operators must disclose that the service is AI, follow suicide and self-harm referral protocols, and not present the service as licensed mental health care. For minors they must block sexual content and romantic role-play, avoid unpredictable engagement rewards, and provide privacy and parental tools. The Attorney General enforces it, with no private right of action and penalties of up to $1,000 per violation and $500,000 per operator.
properties.source_title: Iowa Legislature – 2026 Iowa Acts ch. 1068 (SF 2417)
properties.analysis_title: Iowa Capital Dispatch (via News From The States) – commentary on Iowa's new AI law

properties.title: Kansas – HB 2313 ban on DeepSeek and foreign-adversary AI on state devices
properties.summary: Signed April 8, 2025. State employees may not access DeepSeek or other AI platforms controlled by countries of concern (China, Cuba, Iran, North Korea, Russia, Venezuela) on state devices, and agencies must block them on state networks. Existing accounts must be deleted, except those used for law enforcement and cybersecurity.
properties.source_title: Kansas Legislature – HB 2313 (2025) bill page
properties.analysis_title: Byte Back (Husch Blackwell) – Kansas enacts law banning state use of DeepSeek

properties.title: Kansas – SB 186 AI deepfake and child exploitation law
properties.summary: Signed in April 2025 (2025 Session Laws ch. 120) and effective July 1, 2025. It criminalizes AI-generated child sexual abuse material and extends the breach-of-privacy statute to nonconsensual AI-created or altered sexual depictions of identifiable people.
properties.source_title: Kansas Legislature – SB 186 (2025) bill page
properties.analysis_title: Regulations.ai – Kansas SB 186 summary

properties.title: Kentucky – AI-generated child sexual abuse material (HB 366)
properties.summary: Amends KRS 531.335 so that possessing or viewing sexual performances by minors includes computer-generated images, and requires those convicted to serve 85% of their sentence before probation or parole eligibility. Signed 4/13/2026 (Acts Ch. 109) and in effect since mid-July 2026.
properties.source_title: Kentucky General Assembly – 2026 RS HB 366 bill record (Acts Ch. 109)
properties.analysis_title: WKYT – Kentucky law targeting AI child sexual abuse materials takes effect

properties.title: Kentucky – SB 4: state government AI governance
properties.summary: The Commonwealth Office of Technology sets AI policy standards, an AI Governance Committee approves state agency AI use, and agencies must disclose certain AI uses, train employees and report each year to the legislature. The law also covers synthetic media in electioneering communications, with a cause of action and a defense for conspicuous disclosure. Signed 3/24/2025 (Acts Ch. 66).
properties.source_title: Kentucky General Assembly – 2025 RS SB 4 bill record (Acts Ch. 66)

properties.title: Louisiana – AI in political ads (HB 459, Act 806)
properties.summary: Election communications that use AI to alter a candidate's image, likeness, or voice must clearly disclose the AI use. Violations meant to injure a candidate or deceive voters can bring a fine of up to $2,000 and up to two years in prison. Signed June 9, 2026, effective Aug. 1, 2026. A companion law, Act 559 (HB 639), requires a disclosure at the start of campaign robocalls that use AI to imitate a public figure's voice.
properties.source_title: Louisiana State Legislature – HB 459 (Act 806)
properties.analysis_title: Phelps Dunbar – Louisiana targets AI use in political communications and digital content

properties.title: Louisiana – AI sexual imagery & CSAM training (Acts 782 and 211)
properties.summary: Act 782 (HB 119) sets a sentence of 5 to 20 years at hard labor for knowingly creating or possessing AI-generated sexual material depicting minors, and raises nonconsensual AI sexual image offenses from misdemeanors to felonies. Act 211 (SB 110) bars using a child's image to train AI to produce child sexual abuse material. Both took effect Aug. 1, 2026.
properties.source_title: Louisiana State Legislature – HB 119 (Act 782)
properties.analysis_title: Phelps Dunbar – Louisiana targets AI use in political communications and digital content

properties.title: Maine – AI Task Force final report (economy and workforce charge)
properties.summary: Governor Mills created the Maine AI Task Force by executive order in December 2024. Its charge included preparing Maine's economy and workforce for AI's opportunities and risks. The final report, announced October 31, 2025, makes 34 recommendations, including economy and workforce measures that acknowledge possible job disruption from manufacturing to professional services.
properties.source_title: Office of Governor Janet Mills – Task Force Releases Report on Artificial Intelligence in Maine

properties.title: Maine – AI chatbot disclosure in consumer transactions (LD 1727)
properties.summary: Businesses may not use an AI chatbot with consumers in a way that could mislead a reasonable consumer into believing they are dealing with a human, unless the consumer is told otherwise. A violation counts as a violation of the Maine Unfair Trade Practices Act. Enacted in 2025 as Public Law ch. 294.
properties.source_title: Maine Law and Legislative Reference Library – LD 1727 law summary (P.L. 2025, ch. 294)

properties.title: Maine – AI in mental health services (LD 2082)
properties.summary: Only licensed professionals may offer therapy or psychotherapy to the public, including services delivered through AI. Licensees may use AI only for administrative or supplementary support. They may not let it make independent therapeutic decisions or communicate therapeutically with clients, and supplementary use requires the client's written consent. Signed Apr. 13, 2026 as Public Law ch. 687.
properties.source_title: Maine Legislature – LD 2082 chaptered law (P.L. ch. 687)
properties.analysis_title: Maine Law and Legislative Reference Library – LD 2082 law summary

properties.title: Maryland – AI Governance Act of 2024 (SB 818)
properties.summary: State government units must inventory and assess the AI systems they use. The Department of Information Technology must adopt policies and procedures for how agencies develop, procure, deploy, use, and assess AI. Approved May 9, 2024 (Ch. 496); effective July 1, 2024.
properties.source_title: Maryland General Assembly – SB 818 (2024, Ch. 496)

properties.title: Maryland – Election misinformation and deepfakes (SB 141, Ch. 444)
properties.summary: The State Administrator of Elections must act on credible reports of election misinformation or disinformation, including deepfakes, and may publish correct information. The law also bars knowingly or recklessly creating, using, or spreading a deepfake to produce materially false information. Approved May 12, 2026; effective June 1, 2026.
properties.source_title: Maryland General Assembly – SB 141 (2026, Ch. 444)

properties.title: Maryland – HB 1202 (2020) facial recognition in job interviews
properties.summary: The law prohibits employers from using facial recognition services during a job applicant's interview unless the applicant consents by signing a waiver with specified contents. It became law as Chapter 446 on May 8, 2020, without the governor's signature, and took effect October 1, 2020.
properties.source_title: Maryland General Assembly – HB 1202 (2020), Labor and Employment – Use of Facial Recognition Services – Prohibition

properties.title: Maryland – Lighthouse Industries AI upskilling and internship grants
properties.summary: In February 2026 the Maryland Department of Labor announced $4 million to prepare workers for AI and emerging-technology jobs, including a $1.5 million AI internship program and a $1 million upskilling and reskilling grant program requiring partnerships with at least three employers.
properties.source_title: Maryland Department of Labor – Gov. Moore announces investments to prepare Maryland workers for AI and emerging technology economies

properties.title: Maryland – Protection From Predatory Pricing Act (HB 895, Ch. 154)
properties.summary: Food retailers with stores of at least 15,000 sq. ft. and third-party delivery services may not use dynamic pricing or a consumer's surveillance data to set higher prices for tax-exempt food, or use protected-class data to deny consumers benefits. Loyalty programs, promotions and cost-based price differences are among the exemptions. Violations are enforced under the Consumer Protection Act after a notice and 45-day cure period, with no private right of action. Approved Apr. 28, 2026; effective Oct. 1, 2026.
properties.source_title: Maryland General Assembly – HB 895 (2026, Ch. 154)
properties.analysis_title: Greenberg Traurig – Algorithmic pricing under fire: state restrictions on personalized and surveillance pricing

properties.title: Massachusetts – AG advisory on AI
properties.summary: AG Andrea Campbell's April 16, 2024 advisory explains that the state's consumer protection law (Chapter 93A), anti-discrimination laws, and data security laws apply to AI developers, suppliers, and users. It warns against misrepresenting what an AI system can do or how reliable it is, and against using AI that discriminates on protected characteristics.
properties.source_title: Massachusetts Attorney General's Office – AG Campbell issues advisory on AI
properties.analysis_title: Massachusetts AGO – AI advisory text (PDF)

properties.title: Massachusetts – Free statewide AI training with Google
properties.summary: Announced February 26, 2026, a partnership between the MA AI Hub and Google gives all Massachusetts residents free access to the Google AI Professional Certificate and Google Career Certificates, with a focus on workers, students and small businesses. The labor secretary also signaled plans to expand AI skills training through MassHire.
properties.source_title: Mass.gov – Governor Healey and Google announce statewide partnership to provide free AI training

properties.title: Massachusetts – Frontier AI safety provisions in economic development bill (S.3178)
properties.stage: Senate passed H.5576 with S.3178 text July 24, 2026; conference committee appointed July 30, 2026
properties.summary: The Senate's economic development bill (S.3178, adopted July 24, 2026 as its amendment to H.5576) would require large frontier AI developers to adopt safety frameworks, let the attorney general sue violators, and create a commission to study AI regulation and safety. A House–Senate conference committee was appointed July 30, 2026, and the bill is not law. On Sept. 18, 2026, Gov. Healey urged conferees to build on the Senate's AI provisions with independent safety reviews and sooner incident reporting.
properties.source_title: Mass.gov (Office of the Governor) – Healey calls for strong AI safety and transparency protections in Mass Wins Act
properties.analysis_title: NBC Boston – Mass. Senate's $325M economic development bill seeks to add housing, rein in AI

properties.title: Massachusetts – H.77 / S.35 FAIR Act (Fostering Artificial Intelligence Responsibility)
properties.stage: Reported favorably by committee; in House Ways and Means
properties.summary: The FAIR Act would bar employers from relying solely on automated decision systems for hiring, firing and promotion decisions and would require an independent impact assessment before such systems are used. It would also limit how employers collect and use worker data and require written notice before collecting it. The Advanced IT committee reported H.77 favorably on December 24, 2025, and the bill now sits in House Ways and Means.
properties.source_title: Massachusetts Legislature – H.77, An Act fostering artificial intelligence responsibility
properties.analysis_title: Massachusetts AFL-CIO – Joint Committee on Advanced IT hosts hearing on bill to place guardrails on use of AI

properties.title: Michigan – AI in political ads and election deepfakes (HB 5141, 5143–5145, 2023)
properties.summary: This package was signed Nov. 30, 2023 (Public Acts 263–266 of 2023). It requires a disclosure on political ads and pre-recorded calls generated with AI. It also bars distributing materially deceptive media within 90 days of an election unless it carries a disclaimer, and sets sentencing guidelines for violations.
properties.source_title: Michigan Legislature – HB 5141 of 2023 (Public Act 263 of 2023)
properties.analysis_title: MultiState – Michigan AI policy overview

properties.title: Michigan – Protection from Intimate Deep Fakes Act (HB 4047/4048)
properties.summary: Public Act 11 of 2025 (HB 4047) was signed Aug. 26, 2025 and took immediate effect. Creating or sharing intimate deepfakes without consent is a misdemeanor (up to 1 year). It becomes a felony of up to 3 years when aggravating factors apply, such as intent to profit or harass. Victims can sue for damages and seek injunctions.
properties.source_title: Michigan Legislature – Public Act 11 of 2025 (HB 4047)

properties.title: Michigan – SB 760 companion chatbots and minors
properties.stage: Passed Senate Apr. 29, 2026; in House Communications and Technology Committee
properties.summary: SB 760 would bar chatbot operators from offering companionship-simulating features, content that encourages self-harm or secrecy, or sexual content to any user unless the operator actually knows the user is an adult. Customer-service, productivity, clinical and narrow educational tools are excluded. The Attorney General could seek $25,000 per violation, and harmed minors or their parents could sue. The Senate passed a substitute 20–17 on April 29, 2026, and the House referred it that day to its Communications and Technology Committee.
properties.source_title: Michigan Legislature – SB 760 of 2025

properties.title: Minnesota – Election deepfake law (Minn. Stat. § 609.771)
properties.litigation: Kohls v. Ellison (8th Cir. No. 25-1300): on Feb. 9, 2026 the court affirmed denial of a preliminary injunction (one plaintiff lacked standing; the other unreasonably delayed); the merits were not decided.
properties.summary: This 2023 law makes it a crime to knowingly or recklessly spread a deepfake without the depicted person's consent, with intent to injure a candidate or influence an election, within 90 days before a nominating convention or once absentee voting has begun. Repeat offenses within five years carry up to 5 years in prison and a $10,000 fine. In Kohls v. Ellison, the Eighth Circuit on Feb. 9, 2026 affirmed the denial of a preliminary injunction without reaching the merits.
properties.source_title: Minnesota Office of the Revisor of Statutes – Minn. Stat. § 609.771
properties.analysis_title: Hamilton Lincoln Law Institute – Kohls v. Ellison case page

properties.title: Minnesota – HF 1606 nudification technology ban (challenged in court)
properties.litigation: xAI First Amendment challenge (D. Minn.). Per news reports (court orders not retrieved): district court denied preliminary injunction Sept. 2026; 8th Cir. granted injunction pending appeal Oct. 2, 2026.
properties.summary: Signed May 7, 2026 (2026 Laws ch. 72) and effective Aug. 1, 2026. Websites, apps and other services may not let users create realistic fake nude images or videos of identifiable people, and advertising or promoting such tools is also banned. The AG can seek civil penalties of up to $500,000 for each unlawful access, download or use, and depicted people can sue for up to triple damages plus punitive damages. News reports say a federal district court declined to block the law in September 2026, but the Eighth Circuit enjoined it on Oct. 2, 2026 pending xAI's appeal.
properties.source_title: Minnesota Office of the Revisor of Statutes – 2026 Session Laws ch. 72 (HF 1606)
properties.analysis_title: MPR News – US appeals court blocks Minnesota law barring nudified photos in xAI lawsuit
properties.court_status: Reported blocked pending appeal (8th Cir., Oct. 2026, per news reports; court order not yet confirmed)

properties.title: Minnesota – SF 4576/HF 4369 AI displacement notice and transition period
properties.summary: These companion bills would require notice and a transitional employment period for workers displaced by AI, with penalties for noncompliance. The Senate Labor Committee recommended SF 4576 as amended on April 7, 2026, and re-referred it to State and Local Government.
properties.source_title: Minnesota Office of the Revisor of Statutes – SF 4576 (2026)
properties.analysis_title: MultiState – AI Workforce Protection Bills Emerge as States Weigh Job Displacement Risks

properties.title: Mississippi – AI Regulation (AIR) Task Force (SB 2426)
properties.summary: This 2025 law created a legislative task force with seven voting members that studies AI and reports annually until it dissolves on Dec. 31, 2027. Its first report, adopted Jan. 13, 2026, recommended a statutory definition of AI and chatbot disclosure by state and local agencies. The Legislature then enacted an AI definition in HB 1723, signed March 9, 2026 and effective July 1, 2026.
properties.source_title: Mississippi PEER Committee – AIR Task Force first annual report (Jan. 13, 2026)
properties.analysis_title: Regulations.ai – Mississippi HB 1723 (2026)

properties.title: Mississippi – AI education and workforce MOU with NVIDIA
properties.summary: Under a June 18, 2025 memorandum of understanding with NVIDIA, Mississippi's community colleges, universities and technical institutions will offer AI programs using NVIDIA Deep Learning Institute resources, coordinated with the Mississippi Artificial Intelligence Network and AccelerateMS.
properties.source_title: Office of Governor Tate Reeves – Mississippi to advance AI education, innovation and workforce development with NVIDIA

properties.title: Mississippi – Executive Order 1584 on AI
properties.summary: Gov. Reeves issued the state's first AI executive order on Jan. 8, 2025. It directs the Department of Information Technology Services to inventory AI that state agencies use or plan to use, review agency AI practices and procurement, and develop policy recommendations for responsible AI use that protects residents' privacy and security.
properties.source_title: Office of Governor Tate Reeves – Executive Order No. 1584 on artificial intelligence (press release)

properties.title: Missouri – Executive Order 26-02 AI workforce and education
properties.summary: Governor Kehoe's Executive Order 26-02 (January 13, 2026) has the Department of Higher Education and Workforce Development evaluate AI training at public colleges and launch AI-focused degrees, certifications, apprenticeships and rapid retraining. Reports and recommendations are due by November 30, 2026.
properties.source_title: Missouri Secretary of State – Executive Order 26-02

properties.title: Montana – HB 178 Limits on Government Use of AI
properties.summary: State and local government entities may not use AI for cognitive behavioral manipulation, for classifying people in ways that cause unlawful discrimination or disparate impact, for malicious purposes, or for surveillance of public spaces, with limited exceptions such as locating missing or wanted people. Signed May 5, 2025 (Ch. 427, Laws of 2025).
properties.source_title: Montana Legislature – MCA § 2-21-102 (enacted by HB 178, Ch. 427, L. 2025)
properties.analysis_title: Montana Free Press Capitol Tracker – HB 178

properties.title: Montana – SB 212 Right to Compute Act
properties.summary: Creates a statutory right to privately own and use computational resources for lawful purposes. Government restrictions must be demonstrably necessary and narrowly tailored to a compelling interest. The act also addresses AI systems that control critical infrastructure. Signed April 16, 2025 (Ch. 150, Laws of 2025).
properties.source_title: Montana Legislature – MCA § 2-10-204, Right to compute (enacted by SB 212, Ch. 150, L. 2025)
properties.analysis_title: Montana Free Press Capitol Tracker – SB 212

properties.title: Nebraska – LB 525 Conversational Artificial Intelligence Safety Act
properties.summary: The Legislature folded the Conversational AI Safety Act (LB 1185) into LB 525, and Gov. Pillen approved it on April 14, 2026. The AI provisions apply from July 1, 2027. Operators must disclose AI when a user could believe they are talking to a human, add safeguards for minors, follow self-harm response protocols, and not present the service as professional mental health care. The AG enforces the act with civil penalties of at least $1,000 per violation, capped at $500,000 per operator.
properties.source_title: Nebraska Legislature – LB 525 slip law (approved Apr. 14, 2026)
properties.analysis_title: Nebraska Unicameral Update – LB 1185 chatbot provisions added to LB 525

properties.title: Nevada – AB 406 AI in Mental and Behavioral Health Care
properties.summary: AI providers may not offer systems programmed to deliver professional mental or behavioral health care, or claim that their AI can act as a therapist. Clinicians may not use AI in direct patient care, but may use it for administrative tasks if they review its output. Civil penalties run up to $15,000 per violation. Signed June 5, 2025, effective July 1, 2025.
properties.source_title: Nevada Legislature (NELIS) – AB 406 (2025)
properties.analysis_title: Wilson Sonsini – Nevada passes law limiting AI use for mental and behavioral healthcare

properties.title: New Hampshire – AI chatbots and child endangerment (HB 143)
properties.summary: A chatbot owner or operator commits endangering the welfare of a child if it directs a communication to a child knowing the communication is meant to get the child to imminently engage in sexual conduct, illegal drug or alcohol use, self-harm or suicide, or violence against others. Operators are also civilly liable for liquidated damages of at least $1,000 per violation, but only the attorney general may sue, after giving the operator 90 days to provide satisfactory assurances of a cure. Approved Aug. 1, 2025 (ch. 270); effective Jan. 1, 2026.
properties.source_title: New Hampshire General Court – HB 143 chaptered final version (Chapter 270, 2025)

properties.title: New Hampshire – Deepfake fraud (HB 1432)
properties.summary: Knowingly creating, distributing, or presenting a deepfake of an identifiable person to embarrass, harass, entrap, defame, extort, or otherwise cause financial or reputational harm is a class B felony. The law also creates a private right of action and bars lobbyists who have used deepfakes from registering. Enacted in 2024 as Chapter 243; effective Jan. 1, 2025.
properties.source_title: New Hampshire General Court – RSA 638:26-a, Fraudulent Use of Deepfakes (2024, 243:1)
properties.analysis_title: Akin – New Hampshire imposes new regulations on AI and criminalizes deepfakes

properties.title: New Jersey – A5316 Artificial Intelligence Workforce Transition Act
properties.summary: Introduced June 23, 2026, A5316 would require employers with 100 or more employees to give the state 90 days' notice before deploying AI expected to cut or restructure 25 or more jobs, with penalties of up to $3,000 per affected worker. It would add 26 weeks of unemployment benefits for certified AI-displaced workers in training, create an AI Displacement Account in the Workforce Development Partnership Fund, and offer retention and retraining tax credits.
properties.source_title: New Jersey Legislature – Assembly Bill A5316 (introduced text)
properties.analysis_title: MultiState – AI Workforce Protection Bills Emerge as States Weigh Job Displacement Risks

properties.title: New Jersey – DCR guidance on algorithmic discrimination
properties.summary: Guidance issued in January 2025 by the NJ Attorney General and Division on Civil Rights explains that the Law Against Discrimination covers automated decision tools used in employment, housing, credit, public accommodations and contracting. Employers and others can be liable for disparate impact without any intent to discriminate, and using a vendor-built tool is no defense. The guidance suggests impact assessments and independent pre- and post-deployment bias audits but creates no new legal requirements.
properties.source_title: NJ Office of the Attorney General / Division on Civil Rights – Guidance on Algorithmic Discrimination and the LAD (Jan. 2025, PDF)
properties.analysis_title: Littler – AI in the Garden State

properties.title: New Jersey – DOL guidance on AI literacy in the workforce system
properties.summary: Workforce notice WD-PY25-14 (April 20, 2026) encourages state and local workforce boards to use WIOA funds for AI literacy and training, including for dislocated workers, and adopts the U.S. DOL AI Literacy Framework's core competencies. It also suggests AI literacy screening at intake and AI content in work-based learning.
properties.source_title: New Jersey Department of Labor – WD-PY25-14: AI in the New Jersey Workforce Development System

properties.title: New Jersey – Deceptive deepfake law (A3540/S2544)
properties.summary: P.L.2025, c.40, signed and effective Apr. 2, 2025, targets realistic AI-made fake audio or video. Creating or using such media to commit or further a crime is a third-degree crime (with fines up to $30,000), and knowingly or recklessly sharing it is a fourth-degree crime. Victims can sue for damages of at least $1,000 per violation, punitive damages and attorney's fees, with exceptions for satire, news reporting and certain platforms.
properties.source_title: NJ Legislature – P.L.2025, c.40 (A3540 ACS 3R) chaptered text
properties.analysis_title: Akin – NJ Enacts Law Against Deceptive AI Deepfakes

properties.title: New Jersey – Fair Price Protection Act (surveillance pricing ban)
properties.effective: Main prohibition Aug. 1, 2027; shelf-label moratorium begins Feb. 1, 2027
properties.summary: Makes it an unlawful practice under the Consumer Fraud Act to vary grocery and other foodstuff prices based on a shopper's personal data. Publicly disclosed discounts and qualifying loyalty programs are still allowed. The law also starts a one-year moratorium on new electronic shelf labels on Feb. 1, 2027. Gov. Sherrill signed it on July 23, 2026 (P.L.2026, c.55), and the main prohibition takes effect Aug. 1, 2027.
properties.source_title: NJ Governor's Office – Gov. Sherrill signs Fair Price Protection Act (July 23, 2026)
properties.analysis_title: Lowenstein Sandler – NJ Fair Price Protection Act

properties.title: New Jersey – S1840 Responsible AI Advancement and Workforce Protection Act
properties.summary: S1840 would create an AI Horizon Fund, financed partly by a 5% assessment on gross AI revenue, to pay for worker retraining and community resilience. Employers with 100 or more employees whose AI deployment leads to layoffs would file an AI Impact Disclosure, and AI-displaced workers would get 13 extra weeks of unemployment benefits.
properties.source_title: New Jersey Legislature – Senate Bill S1840 (introduced text)

properties.title: New Jersey – Workplace AI bill (S4075)
properties.stage: Reported by Senate Labor Committee Oct. 1, 2026; referred to Senate Budget and Appropriations Committee
properties.summary: S4075 would bar employers and public entities from using electronic monitoring tools, automated employment decision systems, or automated benefit and service decision systems until an independent impact assessment (or a Labor Department review for public employers) approves them. Workers and their unions would get 60 days' written notice, with limits on certain surveillance, meaningful human review of decisions, and a right to contest adverse decisions; public employees displaced by these systems would receive severance, health benefits, recall rights and retraining. Introduced May 4, 2026, it was reported favorably by the Senate Labor Committee on Oct. 1, 2026 and referred to Senate Budget and Appropriations.
properties.source_title: New Jersey Legislature – S4075 (2026), introduced bill text
properties.analysis_title: Philadelphia Inquirer – NJ bill on AI and workers (Oct. 2026)

properties.title: New Mexico – HB 182 AI Disclosure in Election Ads
properties.summary: Political ads containing 'materially deceptive media' (AI-generated images, video or audio showing a real person saying or doing something they did not, published without consent) must carry a clear disclaimer, enforced through Campaign Reporting Act civil penalties; audio-only ads must speak it at the start, at the end, and at least every two minutes if longer than two minutes. Separately, knowingly distributing such media within 90 days of an election to mislead voters without a disclaimer is a misdemeanor (a fourth-degree felony for a second conviction), and prosecutors, the depicted person, candidates or voter groups can seek injunctions. Signed March 5, 2024 (Laws 2024, ch. 57).
properties.source_title: New Mexico Legislature – HB 182 (2024), chaptered
properties.analysis_title: BABL AI – New Mexico enacts AI disclosure law for campaign ads

properties.title: New York City – Local Law 144 (AEDT bias audits)
properties.summary: NYC employers and employment agencies using automated employment decision tools must have an independent bias audit within the prior year, post a summary of the results, and notify candidates. DCWP can impose civil penalties of $500 to $1,500 per violation, with each day counted separately. A December 2025 State Comptroller audit found DCWP's complaint-driven enforcement ineffective, and DCWP agreed to most of the recommendations, including better complaint routing and stronger investigations.
properties.source_title: NYS Office of the State Comptroller – Enforcement of Local Law 144 audit (Dec. 2, 2025)
properties.analysis_title: DLA Piper – Critical audit of NYC AI hiring law (Jan. 2026)

properties.title: New York – A3719 "robot tax" on AI-displaced workers
properties.summary: The proposed robot tax act would impose a corporate tax surcharge when technology such as AI replaces a worker, equal to the state and local taxes tied to that worker's final-year wages. It was re-referred to the Assembly Ways and Means Committee on January 7, 2026.
properties.source_title: New York State Senate – Assembly Bill A3719 (2025-2026)

properties.title: New York – A9533A Automation Displacement Protection Act
properties.summary: A9533A would require employers with 50 or more full-time employees in New York to give at least 90 days' written notice before a technological displacement affecting 25 employees or 25% of the workforce, whichever is less. The notice would start a 90-day transition period with continued work or equivalent wages, or employer-paid approved retraining. Violators could lose state grants, loans and tax incentives for five years and face penalties up to $10,000 per day for willful violations. Amended on April 23, 2026, it was referred to the Assembly Codes Committee on April 28, 2026.
properties.source_title: New York State Senate – Assembly Bill A9533 (2025-2026)

properties.title: New York – A9581B/S8706B annual AI workforce impact reports
properties.stage: Passed both chambers (June 2026); not yet delivered to the governor
properties.summary: Passed by both houses (Senate vote June 4, 2026) but not yet delivered to the Governor, this bill would require businesses with more than 50 employees, or any publicly traded company, to report annually to the Department of Labor by March 1 on workers displaced, hired or with changed hours due to AI and on positions left unfilled because of AI. The DOL would publish an aggregate report, and late filers face up to $500 per day after a 90-day cure period.
properties.source_title: New York State Senate – Assembly Bill A9581 (2025-2026)
properties.analysis_title: Thompson Coburn – New York Legislature passes AI workforce impact disclosure bill

properties.title: New York – AI Companion Models safeguards (GBL Art. 47)
properties.summary: AI companion operators must tell users they are not talking to a human, at the start of an interaction and at least every three hours during continued use. They must also detect expressions of suicidal ideation or self-harm and refer users to crisis services. The law (GBL Art. 47, enacted in the FY2026 budget) took effect Nov. 5, 2025, and the AG can seek penalties of up to $15,000 per day, paid into a suicide prevention fund.
properties.source_title: NY Governor's Office – Letter to AI companion companies on safeguard requirements
properties.analysis_title: Fenwick – NY AI Companion Safeguard Law Takes Effect

properties.title: New York – AI training for the state workforce
properties.summary: In April 2026, Governor Hochul expanded responsible-AI training, delivered with InnovateUS, to more than 100,000 state employees alongside the AI Pro generative AI assistant built by the Office of Information Technology Services. Agencies using AI Pro must require the training.
properties.source_title: NYS Office of Information Technology Services – Governor Hochul delivers AI training tool to the state workforce (Apr. 6, 2026)

properties.title: New York – Algorithmic Pricing Disclosure Act
properties.summary: Businesses that set a price with an algorithm using a consumer's personal data must display the label 'THIS PRICE WAS SET BY AN ALGORITHM USING YOUR PERSONAL DATA' (GBL § 349-a), a rule in effect since Nov. 10, 2025. A broader ban, the One Fair Price Act (S8623B/A9349B), passed the Legislature on June 4, 2026 and would replace the disclosure rule. As of mid-October 2026, the Legislature's records show no delivery to or action by Gov. Hochul.
properties.source_title: NY Attorney General – Consumer alert as Algorithmic Pricing Disclosure Act takes effect (Nov. 2025)
properties.analysis_title: Greenberg Traurig – State restrictions on personalized pricing (Sept. 2026)

properties.title: New York – FutureWorks Commission on AI and workers
properties.summary: Governor Hochul launched the FutureWorks Commission on March 19, 2026 to advise on protecting workers' economic security while capturing AI's economic benefits, including real-time tracking of AI's labor-market effects. Membership was announced May 18, 2026: 20 members co-chaired by Tom Perez, Thasunda Brown Duckett and Molly Kinder. Recommendations are due by the end of 2026.
properties.source_title: Office of Governor Kathy Hochul – Governor Hochul announces membership of FutureWorks Commission

properties.title: New York – Kids chatbot safety bill (S9051B/A10379)
properties.stage: Passed both chambers (June 2026); not yet delivered to the governor
properties.summary: Would add GBL Article 48, barring operators from offering 'unsafe AI companion features' to known minors. These include features that simulate companionship, claim to be human, encourage secrecy or isolation, promote self-harm, or produce sexually explicit content. Operators would also have to offer age-determination methods, with AG enforcement and a Jan. 1, 2027 effective date. The bill passed the Senate 60-0 on June 4, 2026 and the Assembly on June 5, 2026, and as of mid-October 2026 it has not been delivered to or acted on by Gov. Hochul.
properties.source_title: NY State Senate – S9051B
properties.analysis_title: Bloomberg Law – AI chatbots for minors face new restrictions under NY bill (June 5, 2026)

properties.title: New York – LOADinG Act limits on AI displacing public employees (Civil Service Law §80(10))
properties.stage: Enacted (ch. 96 of 2025); amended by ch. 711 of 2025 and ch. 86 of 2026 (S8831, signed Feb. 13, 2026)
properties.summary: Civil Service Law §80(10) bars state and local public employers, including public authorities, school districts and BOCES, from using AI systems, as defined in State Technology Law §103-e, in ways that cause employees to be discharged or displaced (including cuts to hours, wages or benefits), transfer employees' existing duties to an AI system, or impair collective bargaining rights. Chapter 711 of 2025 briefly extended these protections to automated decision-making tools, but Chapter 86 of 2026 (S8831, signed Feb. 13, 2026) limited them again to AI systems as defined. The subdivision expires July 1, 2028.
properties.source_title: New York State Senate – Civil Service Law §80 (current text)
properties.analysis_title: Manhattan Institute – New York's LOADinG Act: Protecting public-sector jobs from AI

properties.title: New York – RAISE Act (frontier AI safety)
properties.stage: Enacted; signed Dec. 19, 2025; chapter amendment signed Mar. 27, 2026
properties.summary: Large frontier developers must publish an AI safety framework and transparency reports, and must report critical safety incidents within 72 hours to a new office within the Department of Financial Services. The law covers models trained on more than 10^26 operations, built by developers with over $500M in annual revenue, and the AG can seek penalties of up to $1M for a first violation and $3M for later ones. Hochul signed the original act (ch. 699 of 2025) on Dec. 19, 2025, then signed chapter amendment S8828 (ch. 96 of 2026) on Mar. 27, 2026, which brought it closer to California's SB 53. It takes effect Jan. 1, 2027.
properties.source_title: NY State Senate – S8828 (chapter amendment, ch. 96 of 2026)
properties.analysis_title: Wiley – NY Finalizes RAISE Act

properties.title: New York – S8928 AI Workforce Impact Transparency Act
properties.summary: Introduced January 16, 2026, S8928 would write into law a requirement that WARN notices state whether job losses stem in whole or part from AI or automation, and have the Labor Commissioner keep a database and publish quarterly summaries by sector and location. It would also create a two-year DOL pilot to test compliance and data accuracy; the bill sits in the Senate Labor Committee.
properties.source_title: New York State Legislature – Senate Bill S8928 text

properties.title: New York – Synthetic performer ad disclosure (S8420-A/A8887-B)
properties.summary: Amends GBL § 396-b so that anyone producing a commercial ad must conspicuously disclose a 'synthetic performer' they know the ad uses, meaning an AI-generated human-like figure. Penalties are $1,000 for a first violation and $5,000 for each later one. Hochul signed it on Dec. 11, 2025 (ch. 617), and it took effect June 9, 2026.
properties.source_title: NY State Senate – S8420-A (signed, ch. 617 of 2025)
properties.analysis_title: Cooley – NY Enacts Synthetic Performer Disclosure Law

properties.title: New York – WARN notice AI disclosure
properties.stage: Announced in 2025 State of the State (Jan. 2025); WARN form implementation not confirmed from official DOL pages
properties.summary: Governor Hochul's 2025 State of the State said the Department of Labor would require employers filing WARN layoff notices to state whether a layoff is related to their use of AI, and would connect affected workers to state and local training programs. DOL's public WARN filing instructions and dashboard do not describe the AI field.
properties.source_title: Office of Governor Kathy Hochul – 2025 State of the State Book
properties.analysis_title: Hunton Andrews Kurth – New York WARN Act: No AI-Related Layoffs Reported in First Year

properties.title: North Carolina – EO 24: AI Leadership Council & AI Accelerator
properties.summary: Gov. Stein signed this order on Sept. 2, 2025. It creates an AI Leadership Council of at least 25 members, an AI Accelerator within NCDIT, and AI oversight teams in each Cabinet agency, and it calls for AI literacy training for the public, including on AI-driven fraud and scams. The Council's Statewide AI Strategic Roadmap recommends a comprehensive policy package to protect residents in the 2027 legislative cycle.
properties.source_title: NC Governor's Office – Executive Order No. 24
properties.analysis_title: NC Department of Information Technology – Statewide AI Strategic Roadmap (AI Leadership Council)

properties.title: North Carolina – S 988 Protecting Workers in the Age of AI Act
properties.summary: S 988 would create an AI Workforce Transition Program and Fund at the Department of Commerce, funded with $50 million, to provide retraining and credentials for workers displaced by AI or automation, through community colleges and other partners. Employers receiving state incentives would have to report layoffs attributable to AI; the bill was re-referred to Appropriations on May 5, 2026.
properties.source_title: North Carolina General Assembly – Senate Bill 988 (2025-2026)

properties.title: North Dakota – HB 1167 AI disclosure in political communications
properties.summary: Requires political communications that use AI to impersonate a person's image or voice to carry an AI-generated-content disclaimer. The governor signed it in April 2025. Also in 2025, North Dakota extended its laws on nonconsensual sexual images (HB 1351) and child pornography (HB 1386) to computer-generated content.
properties.source_title: North Dakota Legislative Branch – HB 1167 (2025) bill overview
properties.analysis_title: MultiState – North Dakota overview

properties.title: Ohio – DAS Policy IT-17 Use of AI in state agencies
properties.stage: Issued Dec. 4, 2023; revised version effective Jan. 5, 2026
properties.summary: Ohio DAS Policy IT-17 sets rules for how state agencies under the Governor plan, buy, secure and govern AI. Using generative AI for work needs approval from the agency director or a designee, and new AI software and generative AI data models go to a multi-agency AI Council. Staff and suppliers must disclose when generative AI produces state work, and confidential data such as personal information may not be entered into public or unconstrained generative AI tools.
properties.source_title: Ohio Department of Administrative Services – Policy IT-17: Use of Artificial Intelligence in State of Ohio Solutions
properties.analysis_title: Community Solutions – Ohio DAS releases policy governing use of AI

properties.title: Ohio – K-12 AI policy mandate (HB 96, R.C. 3301.24)
properties.effective: Model policy due Dec. 31, 2025; district policies due July 1, 2026
properties.summary: The FY2026–27 budget (HB 96) added R.C. 3301.24, which required the Department of Education and Workforce to produce a model AI policy by Dec. 31, 2025. Every school district, community school and STEM school had to adopt its own AI-use policy by July 1, 2026, and could adopt the model.
properties.source_title: Ohio Department of Education and Workforce – AI Model Policy

properties.title: Ohio – SB 163 AI-generated CSAM, deepfake identity fraud and watermarking
properties.summary: Would make AI-generated child sexual abuse material a crime, and would bar using a digital replica of a person without consent to induce financial decisions, damage reputations, or depict them sexually. It would also let victims of unlawful replicas sue, and would require watermarks on AI-generated content, enforceable by the Attorney General. The Senate passed it unanimously on May 20, 2026, and it is pending in the House Technology and Innovation Committee.
properties.source_title: Ohio House of Representatives – SB 163 (136th GA)
properties.analysis_title: NBC4 (WCMH) – Ohio Senate passes bill targeting AI child sexual abuse material, deepfakes

properties.title: Oklahoma – AI-generated intimate images (HB 1364)
properties.summary: Extends Oklahoma's revenge-porn statute to AI-generated sexual depictions. The base offense is a misdemeanor, and committing it for financial gain or as a repeat offense is a felony. Gov. Stitt signed it in May 2025, and it took effect Nov. 1, 2025.
properties.source_title: Oklahoma House of Representatives – Hasenbeck's AI revenge porn bill (HB 1364) signed into law (May 7, 2025)
properties.analysis_title: BABL AI – Oklahoma enacts AI revenge porn law

properties.title: Oklahoma – Responsible Technology in Schools Act (SB 1734)
properties.stage: Enacted 2026 (signature date not confirmed from official record)
properties.effective: District AI policies required before the 2027–28 school year
properties.summary: Creates the Oklahoma Responsible Technology in Schools Act. Student-facing AI tools must be used under a classroom educator's guidance, districts must tell parents when AI is used in the classroom and let them opt their child out, and the State Department of Education must issue guidance on responsible AI use. Local school boards must adopt district AI policies before the 2027–28 school year.
properties.source_title: Oklahoma Legislature – SB 1734 (enrolled)
properties.analysis_title: Lightspeed – SB 1734 is now law

properties.title: Oregon – SB 1546 AI Companions
properties.summary: AI companion operators must disclose that users are interacting with AI and must keep a protocol to detect suicidal or self-harm ideation and refer users to crisis lifelines, publishing an annual report on those referrals. For known or suspected minors, operators must give break reminders at least every three hours and take reasonable steps to prevent romantic or sexual content and simulated emotional dependence. Injured users can sue for the greater of actual damages or $1,000 per violation. Gov. Kotek signed it on March 31, 2026 (Or. Laws 2026, ch. 85), and it takes effect Jan. 1, 2027.
properties.source_title: Oregon Legislature – Oregon Laws 2026, Chapter 85 (SB 1546)
properties.analysis_title: Dechert (via Mondaq) – Cyber Bits Issue 93: Oregon SB 1546

properties.title: Pennsylvania – Digital forgery crime (SB 649, Act 35 of 2025)
properties.summary: Adds 18 Pa.C.S. § 4101.1, which makes it a crime to create a forged digital likeness of a real person and distribute it as genuine with intent to defraud or injure. It is a first-degree misdemeanor, or a third-degree felony when part of a scheme to defraud, coerce or steal. Gov. Shapiro signed SB 649 on July 7, 2025 (Act 35), and it took effect 60 days later.
properties.source_title: PA Governor's Office – Gov. Shapiro signs new digital forgery law (July 7, 2025)
properties.analysis_title: Justia – Pennsylvania Act 35 of 2025 (text)

properties.title: Pennsylvania – Governor's AI consumer-protection actions (Feb. 2026)
properties.summary: On Feb. 27, 2026, Gov. Shapiro announced a multi-agency AI literacy toolkit and a Department of State process for reporting AI bots that may be practicing a licensed profession without a license. He also created a 12-member AI Enforcement Task Force at the Department of State to evaluate AI companion bots, which shares complaints and referrals with the Attorney General.
properties.source_title: PA Governor – Shapiro takes action to protect Pennsylvanians using AI

properties.title: Pennsylvania – SAFECHAT Act (SB 1090)
properties.summary: Would require operators of AI companion chatbots to disclose that the companion is artificial, keep protocols that block suicide and self-harm content and refer at-risk users to crisis services, and, for minors, add periodic break reminders and block sexually explicit content. It passed the Senate 49-1 on Mar. 17, 2026 and is pending in the House.
properties.source_title: PA Attorney General – Statement on Senate passage of SB 1090 (Mar. 17, 2026)
properties.analysis_title: City & State PA – Lawmakers advance SAFECHAT Act (Mar. 2026)

properties.title: Rhode Island – AI chatbot self-harm protocols (S2195/H7350)
properties.effective: Jan. 1, 2027; annual AG reporting begins July 1, 2027
properties.summary: Operators of AI companion chatbots must keep protocols to detect expressions of suicidal ideation, self-harm or intent to physically harm others and refer users to crisis services, and must tell users they are not talking to a human at the start of an interaction and at least every three hours. The law takes effect Jan. 1, 2027, and operators must file annual reports with the AG starting July 1, 2027. The AG enforces it, with civil penalties of up to $15,000 per day.
properties.source_title: RI General Assembly Press Bureau – AI chatbot safety and AI in mental healthcare bills enacted (6/23/2026)
properties.analysis_title: Transparency Coalition – Rhode Island enacts three new AI laws

properties.title: Rhode Island – AI in mental health care / therapy chatbot ban (H7349/S2197)
properties.summary: Therapy or psychotherapy offered to the public, including through AI, must be conducted by a licensed professional, and clinicians may not let AI make independent therapeutic decisions or set treatment plans. Patients must be told in writing and give consent before AI provides supplementary support in recorded or transcribed sessions. Enacted in June 2026 and effective on passage; a companion law, H7538/S2570, requires providers to notify patients when AI documents a visit and lets them opt out.
properties.source_title: RI General Assembly – H 7349 Substitute A (enacted version) text
properties.analysis_title: Transparency Coalition – Rhode Island enacts three new AI laws

properties.title: South Carolina – AI-generated CSAM (S. 28, Act 57)
properties.summary: Creates a felony for knowingly producing, distributing, soliciting, or possessing obscene sexual depictions of minors, expressly covering computer-generated and digital images even when no real child exists. Gov. McMaster signed it May 22, 2025 as Act No. 57, effective on signing. A companion bill, S. 29 (Act No. 58), extends sexual-exploitation offenses to morphed images of identifiable minors.
properties.source_title: SC Statehouse – S. 28 bill status (Act No. 57)
properties.analysis_title: SC Statehouse – S. 29 bill status (Act No. 58)

properties.title: South Dakota – SB 164 (2025) election deepfakes
properties.summary: Signed March 25, 2025, the law bars spreading a deepfake of a candidate within 90 days of an election when the person intends to injure the candidate and knows or should know it is a deepfake. Violations are a Class 1 misdemeanor, and the AG, the candidate, or the person depicted can seek an injunction and damages. Satire and parody are exempt, and carrying a prescribed AI-manipulation disclosure is an affirmative defense.
properties.source_title: South Dakota Legislature – SB 164 (2025) enrolled text
properties.analysis_title: Akin – SD cracks down on unlabeled deepfakes

properties.title: South Dakota – SB 41 (2026) sexual deepfakes felony
properties.summary: Signed March 16, 2026 and effective July 1, 2026, the law makes it a Class 5 felony (up to five years in prison) to knowingly create or distribute realistic digitally fabricated nude or sexual images of an identifiable person. It does this by adding the offense to South Dakota's criminal invasion-of-privacy statute.
properties.source_title: South Dakota Legislature – SB 41 (2026) enrolled text
properties.analysis_title: South Dakota Searchlight – deepfakes felony bill signed

properties.title: Tennessee – AI may not pose as a mental health professional (SB 1580)
properties.summary: Bars developers and deployers from advertising or claiming that an AI system is, or can act as, a qualified mental health professional. A violation counts as an unfair or deceptive practice under the TN Consumer Protection Act, with a private right of action and a $5,000 civil penalty per violation. Signed 4/1/2026 as Public Chapter 647, effective 7/1/2026.
properties.source_title: Tennessee Department of Health – 2026 legislative updates (Public Chapter 647)
properties.analysis_title: Healthcare Law Insights (Keegan & Vergara) – Tennessee bars AI from posing as mental health professionals

properties.title: Tennessee – ELVIS Act (voice & likeness)
properties.summary: Expands Tennessee's publicity-rights law to protect a person's voice, including AI-simulated voices. It creates liability for unauthorized use, for distribution, and for tools whose primary purpose is replicating a specific person. Signed 3/21/2024 and effective 7/1/2024.
properties.source_title: Tennessee Governor's Office – Gov. Lee signs ELVIS Act into law (3/21/2024)
properties.analysis_title: Manatt – ELVIS Act analysis

properties.title: Tennessee – TACIR studies of AI and child safety (Pub. Ch. 1066 & 1082)
properties.stage: Enacted; PC 1066 study under way as of Sept. 2026
properties.summary: Two 2026 laws direct the Tennessee Advisory Commission on Intergovernmental Relations to study AI risks, especially to children, and options to reduce them (PC 1066 from SB 1493; PC 1082 from SB 1700, which as filed would have restricted harmful chatbots for minors). The PC 1066 study is under way as of September 2026, and PC 1082's study begins once it is finished.
properties.source_title: Tennessee Advisory Commission on Intergovernmental Relations – Sept. 2026 AI and child safety memo

properties.title: Texas – HB 149 Texas Responsible AI Governance Act (TRAIGA)
properties.summary: Bans developing or deploying AI intended to incite self-harm, harm to others, or crime, to unlawfully discriminate (disparate impact alone does not show intent), or to produce prohibited sexual content or deepfakes. Government entities may not use AI for social scoring or rights-infringing biometric identification, and healthcare providers must disclose AI use to patients. Effective January 1, 2026, the AG enforces it exclusively, with a 60-day cure period and penalties of up to $200,000 per uncurable violation, and opened an online AI complaint portal on September 1, 2026.
properties.source_title: Texas Attorney General – Texas Responsible Artificial Intelligence Governance Act (consumer AI rights and complaint page)
properties.analysis_title: Cloud Security Alliance – research note on the TRAIGA complaint portal

properties.title: Texas – SB 1188 AI in Diagnosis & EHR Requirements
properties.effective: AI duties Sept. 1, 2025; EHR storage Jan. 1, 2026
properties.summary: Practitioners who use AI for diagnostic or treatment recommendations based on patient records must review AI-generated records under medical-records standards and disclose that use to patients; these duties took effect September 1, 2025. Covered entities must also physically store electronic health records in the U.S. or its territories starting January 1, 2026.
properties.source_title: Texas Legislature Online – SB 1188 (89R, enrolled)
properties.analysis_title: Texas Medical Association – SB 1188 summary

properties.title: Texas – Workforce Investment Council report: Workforce Impacts of Artificial Intelligence
properties.summary: In June 2026 the Texas Workforce Investment Council published a report, under its statutory workforce-research role, finding that AI mainly threatens cognitive white-collar work while skilled trades face strong near-term demand. The report recommends reskilling and upskilling in AI literacy and human skills. It also notes about 49,135 AI-attributed job cuts nationally through April 2026.
properties.source_title: Texas Workforce Investment Council – Workforce Impacts of Artificial Intelligence (June 2026)

properties.title: Utah – Artificial Intelligence Policy Act (as amended)
properties.stage: Enacted; amended by 2025 SB 226 and SB 332 and 2026 HB 320
properties.effective: Ch. 72 (Office/learning lab) repeals July 1, 2027 under SB 332; HB 320 changes effective May 6, 2026; ch. 75 disclosures have no repeal date
properties.summary: Businesses using generative AI must disclose it when a consumer clearly asks, and licensed professionals must prominently disclose 'high-risk' AI interactions; 2025 SB 226 moved these duties into a separate chapter with no end date. The Act's Office of AI Policy and AI learning laboratory (regulatory sandbox) are set to repeal July 1, 2027 under 2025 SB 332. 2026 HB 320 (effective May 6, 2026) reworked the Office's duties and the sandbox's regulatory agreements.
properties.source_title: Utah Legislature – SB 332 (2025) enrolled text
properties.analysis_title: Vaquill: Utah AI law explained from the statute

properties.title: Utah – Executive Order 2026-08 Pro-Human AI and state workforce AI literacy
properties.summary: Executive Order 2026-08, signed October 6, 2026, requires applicable state employees to complete AI literacy training and directs the Division of Technology Services and Division of Human Resource Management to build a training strategy, with specialized training for agency AI leads. It prioritizes upskilling existing staff to work alongside AI.
properties.source_title: Office of Governor Spencer J. Cox – Executive Order 2026-08
properties.analysis_title: GovTech – Utah Governor Signs Executive Order for Pro-Human AI

properties.title: Utah – HB 276 AI Modifications (Digital Voyeurism Prevention & Content Provenance)
properties.effective: Most duties Jan. 1, 2027; device duties for devices made on or after Jan. 1, 2028
properties.summary: Generative AI services may not distribute counterfeit intimate images without verified consent, and platforms must remove such images within 48 hours of a valid notice. Large platforms must detect and display content provenance data, large generative AI providers and capture-device makers must embed latent disclosures, and the Division of Consumer Protection can fine up to $2,500 per violation. Acted on by the governor March 24, 2026; most duties begin January 1, 2027, with device duties covering devices made on or after January 1, 2028.
properties.source_title: Utah Legislature – HB 276 (2026) enrolled text
properties.analysis_title: Regulations.ai – Utah HB 276 summary

properties.title: Utah – HB 452 Mental Health Chatbots
properties.summary: Mental health chatbot suppliers must clearly disclose that the chatbot is AI and not a human. They generally may not sell or share users' health information or inputs, and in-chat ads must be labeled and may not be targeted using user input. The Division of Consumer Protection can impose fines of up to $2,500 per violation. Signed March 25, 2025 and effective May 7, 2025.
properties.source_title: Utah Legislature – HB 452 (2025) enrolled text
properties.analysis_title: Wilson Sonsini – Utah enacts mental health chatbot law

properties.title: Vermont – AI in mental health services (H.816, Act 156)
properties.summary: Companies may not offer mental health services to the public, including through AI, unless a licensed mental health professional provides them. Clinicians may still use HIPAA-compliant AI tools whose output they review and approve. Violations are treated as Consumer Protection Act violations, enforceable by the AG and by private parties. Signed June 17, 2026 and effective on passage.
properties.source_title: Vermont Legislature – H.816 bill status (Act 156)
properties.analysis_title: Vermont Legislature – Act 156 as enacted (PDF)

properties.title: Vermont – Synthetic media in elections (S.23, Act 75)
properties.summary: Requires a clear disclosure on deceptive synthetic media of candidates, or synthetic media meant to sway an election with materially false content, when it is distributed within 90 days before an election. Satire, parody, and bona fide newscasts are exempt. Knowing violations carry fines of up to $1,000, and misrepresented candidates may seek injunctions. Gov. Scott signed it March 5, 2026, effective immediately.
properties.source_title: Vermont Legislature – S.23 bill status (Act 75)
properties.analysis_title: Vermont Legislature – Act 75 Act Summary (PDF)

properties.title: Virginia – EO 22: Rapid-Response AI Task Force
properties.summary: Gov. Spanberger signed this order on 9/18/2026. It sets up a data center accountability framework and an AI task force to assess AI risks to the workforce, privacy and cybersecurity and to recommend executive or legislative action. AI policies issued under former Gov. Youngkin's EO 30 stay in effect until the task force replaces them.
properties.source_title: Virginia Governor's Office – Executive Order 22 (2026)
properties.analysis_title: Greenberg Traurig – EO 22 analysis

properties.title: Virginia – Synthetic media in political ads (HB 868, carried to 2027)
properties.stage: Reported as continued to the 2027 session (not confirmed from official LIS history)
properties.summary: HB 868, titled 'Political campaign advertisements; synthetic media, penalty,' would require political campaign ads that use synthetic (AI-generated) media to carry a disclosure, with penalties for violations. It was on the House Privileges and Elections Campaigns and Candidates subcommittee's January 27, 2026 docket. Reports say it was continued to 2027, but the official bill history could not be loaded to confirm this.
properties.source_title: Virginia LIS – HB 868 (2026) bill details
properties.analysis_title: FastDemocracy – VA HB 868 status history

properties.title: Virginia – Virginia Has Jobs AI Career Launch Pad
properties.summary: Launched July 15, 2025 by Governor Youngkin with Virginia Works and Google, the AI Career Launch Pad gives Virginians access to Google AI Essentials courses and to Google Career Certificates, with Virginia Works distributing Career Certificate scholarships. It also lists other no-cost and low-cost training. The release cites about 31,000 AI-related job listings in Virginia.
properties.source_title: Office of the Governor of Virginia – AI Career Launch Pad announcement

properties.title: Virginia – Virginia Works report: AI and Its Implications for Virginia's Workforce
properties.summary: On June 15, 2026, Virginia Works, the state Department of Workforce Development and Advancement, released a statewide analysis of AI's effects on the state's workforce. The report stresses that AI exposure is not the same as job loss and that exposure now reaches higher-wage fields such as finance, legal services and computer science. It highlights durable skills such as communication and critical thinking.
properties.source_title: Virginia Works – Artificial Intelligence and Its Implications for Virginia's Workforce

properties.title: Washington – AI Task Force AI and Labor Survey Report 2026
properties.summary: The Attorney General's AI Task Force, created by SB 5838, commissioned a survey of 582 Washington workers conducted between December 2025 and January 2026. In the survey, 80% of respondents had negative feelings about AI in their jobs, and 12% had lost a job in the past year; 55% of those said AI was a primary or contributing factor. The survey accompanied the Task Force's final report, released July 1, 2026.
properties.source_title: Washington State Attorney General – Washington State AI & Labor Survey Report 2026
properties.analysis_title: Washington State Attorney General – Washington State AI Task Force releases final report

properties.title: Washington – HB 1170 AI Content Disclosure / Provenance
properties.summary: Generative AI providers with over 1 million monthly users that are publicly available in Washington must embed hard-to-remove latent provenance data in image, video, or audio content their systems create or materially alter, where commercially and technically reasonable. The AG alone enforces it as a Consumer Protection Act violation. Signed March 24, 2026 (Ch. 167, Laws of 2026), effective February 1, 2027.
properties.source_title: Washington State Legislature – HB 1170 bill summary (C 167 L 26)
properties.analysis_title: Washington State Legislature – HB 1170 session law (Ch. 167, Laws of 2026)

properties.title: Washington – HB 1622 public-employee bargaining over AI
properties.stage: Passed House in 2025 but returned to Rules; referred to Rules Feb. 3, 2026
properties.summary: HB 1622 would make matters related to public employers' use of artificial intelligence a subject of collective bargaining. The House passed it 58-38 on March 8, 2025, but it was returned to House Rules. In 2026 the House Appropriations Committee recommended a second substitute on January 28, and the bill was referred to Rules on February 3 without a floor vote.

properties.title: Washington – HB 1672 workplace technology and electronic monitoring (with HB 2144)
properties.summary: HB 1672 would limit private employers' electronic monitoring of employees and regulate the use of automated decision systems, such as facial, gait or emotion recognition, in employment decisions. It was reintroduced on January 12, 2026 and remains in House Appropriations. A companion 2026 bill, HB 2144, would require advance written notice before AI tools or electronic monitoring are used in performance evaluations.

properties.title: Washington – HB 2225 AI Companion Chatbots
properties.summary: Companion chatbots must disclose they are AI at the start of each interaction and every three hours (hourly for minors), and may not claim to be human. Operators must block sexual content and manipulative tactics for minors and keep self-harm detection and referral protocols. Enforced under the Consumer Protection Act. Signed March 24, 2026 (Ch. 168), effective January 1, 2027.

properties.title: Washington – SB 5886 Personality Rights / Forged Digital Likenesses
properties.summary: Gives people a property right in their 'forged digital likeness', meaning realistic digitally created or altered images or voice recordings that are likely to deceive. Unauthorized commercial use is treated as infringement, with a $3,000 civil penalty plus damages, profits, and noneconomic damages. Signed March 16, 2026 (Ch. 69), effective June 11, 2026.

properties.title: Wisconsin – 2023 Act 123 AI disclosure in political ads
properties.summary: AB 664, enacted March 21, 2024, requires political audio and video communications that contain synthetic media, meaning content produced in whole or in part by generative AI, to carry prescribed 'generated by AI' disclosures. The Elections Commission may adopt limited exceptions by rule. Each intentional violation carries a forfeiture of up to $1,000.

properties.title: Wisconsin – 2025 Act 34 synthetic intimate representations
properties.summary: SB 33 was enacted October 2, 2025, published October 3, and took effect the day after publication. It defines a 'synthetic intimate representation' and makes it a crime to post or distribute a realistic, technologically generated intimate depiction of an identifiable person with intent to coerce, harass, or intimidate them.

properties.title: Wisconsin – Governor's Task Force on Workforce and AI advisory action plan (EO 211)
properties.summary: Governor Evers created the Task Force on Workforce and Artificial Intelligence through Executive Order #211 in August 2023. Its July 2024 advisory action plan makes recommendations in education, government, workforce development and economic development. These include extending worker-transition help to AI-affected workers, adding a layoff aversion program and expanding AI training grants.
